core_principles: Walking forward lunges (WFL) elicit a short eccentric contraction of the hamstrings at the start of the stance phase, followed by concentric action.
Jumping forward lunges (JFL) involve an initial isometric contraction of the hamstrings, followed by a strong concentric contraction during push-off.
The rectus femoris undergoes eccentric contraction during the early stance of a jumping lunge, transitioning to concentric and then eccentric again before push-off.
Gastrocnemius activity peaks around mid-stance (45-50%) for both lunge variations, but is significantly higher during jumping lunges.
Walking forward lunges are highly effective for improving concentric hamstring strength.
specific_findings: WFL group improved concentric hamstring strength by 35% after six weeks of training, from 92 Nm to 124 Nm (p<0.001).
WFL showed a significant increase in hamstring strength at day two compared to baseline, with a mean strength of 107 Nm (p<0.01).
Immediately after the first training session, quadriceps strength decreased from 171 to 162 Nm (p<0.05) in the WFL group, and from 150 to 132 Nm (p<0.001) in the JFL group.
In WFL, the rectus femoris EMG peaks at approximately 40% of the stance phase, whereas in JFL, it peaks at approximately 60% of the stance phase.
Gastrocnemius EMG peaks at approximately 45% stance in JFL and 50% stance in WFL.
JFL group increased 30-meter sprint performance by 2% (p<0.001 compared to baseline).
Median muscle pain (VAS) immediately after exercise increased from 0 to 1 in WFL, and from 0 to 3.5 in JFL.

The gastrocnemius works eccentrically during most of the stance phase, with EMG peaks in the middle and end of the stance phase to store elastic energy for the concentric push-off.
